samples.text:
The line graph gives information about unemployment rate for three age groups, 16-24, 25-49 and 50-64, in a European country between 2008 and 2020.

The youngest group had the highest unemployment in all the years. In 2008 it was 12.5% and then it rose quickly to 24.5% in 2012, that was the highest point on the graph. After this it fell to 14.5% in 2016 and 11.0% in 2018. But in 2020 it went up again to 17.5%.

The 25-49 group was much lower. It start at 5.0% in 2008 and went up to 9.0% in 2012. Then it decreased to 4.0% in 2018 and rise a little to 6.0% in 2020. The 50-64 group had 3.5% in 2008, which was the lowest. It increased to 7.5% in 2012 and after that it go down slowly to 4.5% in 2018 and 5.0% in 2020.

Overall, all groups was increasing until 2012 and then decreasing, and the young people always had more unemployment than the other groups.
samples.why: Overview present but placed at the end · main trends covered in a list-like way · limited range of linking · several tense and subject-verb agreement errors, though meaning remains clear.

samples.text:
The graph illustrates the percentage of people who were unemployed in three age groups (16-24, 25-49 and 50-64) in one European country over the period from 2008 to 2020.

Overall, young people aged 16 to 24 were by far the most likely to be unemployed at every point. All three groups followed a broadly similar pattern, with unemployment rising until 2012, falling until 2018 and then increasing again in 2020.

Youth unemployment stood at 12.5% in 2008 before almost doubling to a peak of 24.5% in 2012. It then declined steadily to 11.0% in 2018, its lowest level, but jumped back up to 17.5% by 2020.

The rates for the two older groups were much lower and closer together. Among 25 to 49-year-olds, unemployment rose from 5.0% to 9.0% between 2008 and 2012, then fell to 4.0% in 2018, before increasing slightly to 6.0%. The 50-64 group began with the lowest rate of 3.5% and peaked at 7.5% in 2012. Interestingly, this group's rate declined more slowly, so it was actually higher than the 25-49 group in 2016 and 2018, although this situation reversed in 2020.
samples.why: Clear overview of the shared pattern · key features highlighted, including the crossover of older groups · logical organisation · good range of cohesive devices · accurate grammar with very few slips.

samples.text:
The line graph compares unemployment rates across three age brackets, 16-24, 25-49 and 50-64, in a European country from 2008 to 2020.

What stands out most is that the youngest workers consistently faced the highest unemployment, with a rate at least double that of either older group throughout. In addition, the three lines moved broadly in tandem, climbing to a peak in 2012, easing until 2018 and then rising once more by 2020.

Among 16 to 24-year-olds, the rate nearly doubled from 12.5% in 2008 to 24.5% in 2012, the highest figure on the graph. A sustained recovery then brought it down to 11.0% by 2018, only for it to rebound to 17.5% in 2020, the sharpest late increase of any group.

The two older cohorts showed far more modest fluctuations. Unemployment among 25 to 49-year-olds rose from 5.0% to 9.0% by 2012, fell to a low of 4.0% in 2018 and edged up to 6.0% in 2020. The 50-64 group started lowest, at 3.5%, and peaked at 7.5% in 2012; however, because its rate fell more gradually, it briefly exceeded that of the middle group in 2016 and 2018.
samples.why: Skilful selection of key features, including the relative scale and the crossover · clear overview · accurate figures used comparatively · precise vocabulary such as 'cohorts' and 'in tandem' · wide range of error-free structures.
